weeks.title: How attackers actually think
weeks.context:
Security work starts with adversarial thinking. Before you can defend anything, you need to understand how attackers reason: they are looking for the cheapest path to their objective, not the most clever one. That means misconfigurations, unpatched dependencies, weak credentials, and human error are attacked far more often than exotic zero-days.

This week you build that mental model. You learn the attack lifecycle (recon → exploit → persist → exfil), the difference between vulnerability and exploit, and how OWASP Top 10 maps to real breaches. You also set up your lab environment so you have a safe place to practise everything that follows.

The Juice Shop is a deliberately vulnerable Node.js app maintained by OWASP. Every bug in it maps to a real vulnerability class. Finding bugs there is not cheating — it is the point.

items.title: Git — version control from day 1
items.body:
## What Git is
Git is the version-control tool every codebase past day 1 uses. It snapshots your project after every meaningful change so you can: see what changed, undo a mistake, collaborate without overwriting each other, and ship to GitHub.

You will use Git every single day on this track. The five commands below cover ~95% of daily work.

## Install + first-time setup
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
# macOS:    brew install git
# Windows:  download from git-scm.com (or `winget install Git.Git`)
# Linux:    sudo apt install git

git --version
git config --global user.name  'Your Name'
git config --global user.email 'you@example.com'
```

## The five commands you actually use
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
git init                 # turn a folder into a git repo
git add file.py          # stage a change for the next commit
git commit -m 'message'  # snapshot the staged changes
git status               # what's changed since the last commit?
git log --oneline        # the history of snapshots
```

## Push to GitHub
The snippet below shows exactly what to do:

```bash
# After creating an empty repo on github.com:
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOU/your-repo.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

## When you'll see Git next
Every project on this track ships to GitHub. Every checkin you submit is backed by a commit. This is the prerequisite — read it once, refer back to it whenever you're not sure.

items.title: What this environment is — and why before anything else
items.body:
## What it is
You **cannot** practice security tools on your everyday laptop's OS. Two reasons:
1. Half the tools you'll run are flagged as malware (correctly — they're attack tools).
2. You need to break things, and breaking your daily-driver is bad.

The answer: a **virtual machine** with a security-focused OS like **Kali Linux**. Inside the VM you can install / break / re-image as much as you want without touching your host.

## What you'll do today
1. Install **VirtualBox** (Windows / Mac / Linux) OR **WSL2 with Kali** (Windows-only, lighter).
2. Download the Kali VM image (or `wsl --install -d kali-linux`).
3. Boot it.
4. Open the terminal inside Kali and run `nmap --version` → confirm output.

items.title: See it in action — the exact steps, with what you should see
items.body:
## Walkthrough
Do every step.

WINDOWS (WSL path, fastest):
1. Open PowerShell as Admin: `wsl --install -d kali-linux`.
2. Reboot. Open 'Kali Linux' from Start.
3. First-run prompts you for a username + password. Set them.
4. `sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nmap`.
5. `nmap --version`.

MAC / LINUX (VirtualBox path):
1. Install **VirtualBox** from virtualbox.org.
2. Download Kali pre-built VirtualBox VM from kali.org/get-kali.
3. Import into VirtualBox, boot it.
4. Inside the VM: `nmap --version`.

## Verify
PASS:
[x] Kali boots
[x] `nmap --version` prints a version inside Kali

cards.prompt: You should install security tools like nmap directly on your everyday laptop OS.
cards.whenRight: Right — no. Use a VM. Half these tools are flagged by antivirus and you don't want to break your daily-driver.
cards.whenWrong: Use a VM. Daily-driver should stay clean; the VM is your lab.

cards.prompt: WSL2 with Kali is a lighter alternative to a full VirtualBox VM on Windows.
cards.whenRight: Right — WSL2 reuses your kernel, no full hypervisor. Faster boots, less RAM.
cards.whenWrong: Yes — WSL2 is the lightweight option on Windows. VirtualBox is heavier but works everywhere.

cards.prompt: Kali Linux ships with nmap, metasploit and most security tools pre-installed.
cards.whenRight: Right — that's its whole point. A pre-loaded toolkit for security work.
cards.whenWrong: Yes — Kali's the 'batteries included' distro for security work. You install fewer things by hand.

items.title: Deeper dive: The ethics contract — non-negotiable
items.body:
## Deeper dive: The ethics contract — non-negotiable

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **The ethics contract — non-negotiable** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

items.title: Sign and commit your ethics contract
items.body:
[WRITE] STEP 1 — Make the folder.
      cd Desktop
      mkdir vuln-reports
      cd vuln-reports

STEP 2 — Create ETHICS.md.
  In VS Code, new file ETHICS.md. Type:

      # Ethics Contract
      I, [YOUR FULL NAME], commit to:
      1. Only test systems I own or have explicit written permission to test.
      2. Report any vulnerabilities I find through responsible disclosure channels.
      3. Never exfiltrate or modify user data beyond minimal proof-of-concept.
      4. Document every test for transparency.
      
      Signed: [YOUR NAME]
      Date: [TODAY'S DATE]

  Replace [YOUR FULL NAME] and [TODAY'S DATE]. Save.

STEP 3 — In notes.txt write 3 sentences:
  Why does ethical hacking matter? Why do real security companies require this contract?

PASS:
[x] You completed the task described above
[x] You can explain in one sentence what you produced
[x] Your work is committed to your repo

items.title: Login Admin via SQL injection
items.body:
[CODE] STEP 1 — Open the login page (top right account icon).

STEP 2 — In the email field, type:
      ' OR 1=1--
  In the password field, type anything (e.g. 'abc').
  Click Log in.

STEP 3 — YOU SHOULD SEE: you are logged in as admin@juice-sh.op.
  Check the top right corner — your account icon shows the admin email.
  The 'Login Admin' challenge is green on the score board.

STEP 4 — Screenshot showing the admin email at top right.
  Save as 03-loginadmin.png

Now challenge 4: View someone else's basket.

STEP 5 — Log out. Register a new normal account (email: test@test.com, any password).
  Add 1 item to your basket. Go to your basket.

STEP 6 — In Chrome DevTools (F12), Network tab. Reload the basket page.
  Find the request to /rest/basket/N (where N is a number, your basket ID).
  Look at the response — that's your basket data.

STEP 7 — Change N. In the URL bar, go to:
  http://localhost:3000/rest/basket/1
  YOU SHOULD SEE: a different user's basket (admin's, in this case). That's IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference.

STEP 8 — Screenshot the raw JSON of someone else's basket.
  Save as 04-idor.png

items.title: Write reports and push
items.body:
[PRODUCE] STEP 1 — Make a reports/ folder.
      cd Desktop/vuln-reports
      mkdir reports

STEP 2 — Write reports/01-scoreboard.md.
  Use this template for ALL 5 reports:

      # Score Board access via hidden route
      
      **Severity:** Low — informational, but reveals the developer's intent
      **Affected component:** Front-end SPA route `/#/score-board`
      
      ## Steps to reproduce
      1. Navigate to http://localhost:3000
      2. View page source (Ctrl+U)
      3. Find the comment hinting at the route
      4. Navigate to /#/score-board
      
      ## Impact
      Hidden admin/dev pages can leak sensitive information.
      
      ## Suggested fix
      Don't ship hints in comments. Gate the route behind an admin role.
      
      ## Proof
      ![scoreboard](../screenshots/01-scoreboard.png)

STEP 3 — Write the other 4 the same way:
  02-domxss.md (Medium severity — code execution in browser)
  03-loginadmin.md (Critical — full admin compromise via SQLi)
  04-idor.md (High — viewing other users' data)
  05-confidential.md (Medium — leaked internal docs)

STEP 4 — Write README.md.
      # vuln-reports
      My security writeups. Practice begins with OWASP Juice Shop.
      
      ## Ethics
      See ETHICS.md — I only test systems I own or have permission to.
      
      ## Reports
      1. [Score Board access](reports/01-scoreboard.md) — Low
      2. [DOM XSS in search](reports/02-domxss.md) — Medium
      3. [Login Admin via SQLi](reports/03-loginadmin.md) — Critical
      4. [IDOR in /rest/basket](reports/04-idor.md) — High
      5. [Leaked acquisitions doc](reports/05-confidential.md) — Medium

STEP 5 — Push.
  Open the 'create new repository' card. Name: vuln-reports. Public. Create.
      git init
      git add .
      git commit -m "vuln-reports v0.1 — 5 Juice Shop writeups"
      git branch -M main

weeks.context:
Last week you found your first bugs. This week you go deeper into Juice Shop and find 5 more, but more importantly you learn how to document them. A security finding you cannot communicate clearly is worthless. Bug bounty hunters, pentesters, and security engineers all get paid to write clear, reproducible vulnerability reports.

You also learn CVSS scoring this week. CVSS v3.1 lets you score a vulnerability's severity from 0 to 10 based on attack vector, complexity, privileges required, and impact. You should be able to score any bug you find from first principles.

items.title: Deeper dive: What you'll attack

## Deeper dive: What you'll attack

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

1. Take the smallest case of **What you'll attack** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.

weeks.title: Vuln Reports v0.3: TryHackMe — first room

TryHackMe is a guided CTF platform where each room walks you through a real vulnerability or technique in a controlled environment. This week you complete your first room and start building the habit of learning through structured hacking challenges.

The difference between Juice Shop and TryHackMe: Juice Shop is an app you attack, THM is a guided lesson where you follow instructions, answer questions, and learn the underlying technique. Both are essential — Juice Shop builds creative thinking, THM builds systematic knowledge.

This week you also start using a proper methodology. Every pentest has phases: scope, recon, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting. Even in a lab setting, you follow the same phases — it builds muscle memory for real engagements.

weeks.title: Vuln Reports v0.4: Burp Suite + intercepting requests
weeks.context:
Burp Suite is the primary tool for web application security testing. Every professional pentester uses it daily. This week you learn to use it like a professional — not just as a traffic viewer, but as an active testing platform.

The core Burp workflow: intercept request → modify it → send to Repeater → iterate until you find a vulnerability. The Repeater tab is where most web hacking actually happens. You send a request, tweak a parameter, observe the response, adjust, repeat.

This week you also learn HTTP deeply. Not just GET vs POST — you need to understand headers (Authorization, Cookie, Content-Type, CORS headers), status codes (200/301/302/401/403/404/500), and how the request/response cycle works at the byte level. Burp shows you everything; you need to know what you're looking at.

weeks.title: Burp Suite + ZAP — Your Web Testing Workbench
weeks.context:
This week you advance from basic Burp usage to a full web testing workflow. You learn Burp's Scanner (Community has a passive scanner; Pro has active), OWASP ZAP as an open-source alternative, and how to combine automated scanning with manual testing.

Automated scanners find the obvious things fast. Manual testing finds the business logic bugs that scanners miss. A professional web pentest uses both: run the scanner to clear the easy wins, then spend 80% of your time on manual testing of the application's specific functionality.

You also learn OWASP's Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG) this week. It is the definitive manual for web application penetration testing — 12 categories, 91 test cases. You will reference it throughout your career.

items.title: Run a scoped workflow on a legal target
items.body:
[PRODUCE] STEP 1 — Pick a target you are EXPLICITLY allowed to test: your own deployed app, a public bug-bounty program whose scope you've read, or a deliberately-vulnerable practice app (OWASP Juice Shop, DVWA) running locally.

STEP 2 — Set Burp scope precisely. Map the app: walk every page with Intercept off so HTTP history fills, then review the sitemap.

STEP 3 — Pick your top 3 most-promising requests (auth, search, anything with an id) and probe each in Repeater. Use Intruder where a list helps. Cross-check with a ZAP active scan.

STEP 4 — Write BURP-FINDINGS.md: for each issue — the request, the payload, the evidence (response delta/screenshot), severity, and a one-line fix. Even 'no issues found on X, here's what I tried' is a valid, professional entry.

YOU SHOULD SEE: a clean, scoped, reproducible report a real team could act on. That document — not the tool clicks — is what the job actually is.

weeks.title: Exploitation — Real Bugs in Real Apps
weeks.context:
Exploitation is where theory meets practice. This week you move beyond finding vulnerabilities and start exploiting them — in controlled lab environments only. You work through PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs, which are the best free hands-on exploitation training available anywhere.

The goal is not to write exploits from scratch. It is to understand how exploitation chains work: one vulnerability becomes the entry point, another escalates privileges, another exfiltrates data. Real attacks are rarely a single CVE — they are a chain.

You also learn Metasploit this week. Metasploit is a framework for running known exploits against known vulnerable targets. It is not a magic hacking button — it is a library of modules that each implement a specific exploit. Understanding why a Metasploit module works is more important than knowing how to run it.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A SQL injection UNION attack lets you extract data from OTHER tables by combining a second SELECT into the original query's result set. For UNION to work, three conditions must be true. (1) The injection point is in a SELECT statement (UPDATE/DELETE injections need different techniques). (2) You can append `UNION SELECT` to the query — the application returns the results of the SELECT to you (visible somewhere in the response). (3) The two SELECT statements must have the SAME NUMBER of columns and COMPATIBLE column types. Walkthrough: original query is `SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = '$input'`. You inject `' UNION SELECT NULL, NULL --` first to confirm two columns. The `--` comments out the closing quote so the query is valid. Then you replace NULLs with the data you want: `' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users --`. The response now shows usernames and passwords next to product names. If the column count is wrong, the database errors out — you increment until matching. If types do not match, NULL works for any type. UNION is the most efficient SQLi exfiltration technique — one request can dump entire tables.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A SYN scan (`nmap -sS`) and a full connect scan (`nmap -sT`) differ in how nmap completes the TCP handshake. TCP normally goes SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK to open a connection. A SYN scan sends the initial SYN, receives SYN/ACK if the port is open or RST if closed, and then sends RST to abort instead of completing the handshake. The target's application layer never sees the connection — so the target may not log the probe. The SYN scan is faster and stealthier. A full connect scan (`-sT`) completes the three-way handshake (SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK), opens a real TCP connection, then immediately closes it. The target's application accepts the connection, logs it, and you appear in the server logs. When to use each: use `-sS` (default) when you have raw socket permissions (root/admin on the scanner machine) — it requires raw sockets to craft the SYN packets directly. Use `-sT` when you do not have raw socket access (running as a normal user) — it uses the OS's connect() system call which works without privileges. Practical: `-sS` is the default and what you use 95% of the time. `-sT` is fallback when you're in a restricted environment.

weeks.title: Reporting and Communication — The Skill That Pays
weeks.context:
Finding vulnerabilities is 40% of a pentester's job. Communicating them clearly is the other 60%. A security finding that the engineering team cannot understand and act on is worthless. This week you learn to write professional penetration test reports.

A professional pentest report has two sections: an executive summary (for leadership, non-technical, focused on business risk) and a technical findings section (for developers, specific reproduction steps, code-level remediation). You need to write both.

You also learn to triage findings by risk. Not everything is Critical. Severity is based on CVSS; risk is based on severity + likelihood + business impact. A CVSS 9.8 vulnerability on an internal system with no external access has lower risk than a CVSS 6.0 vulnerability on a public-facing payment page.

The most significant is a critical SQL injection vulnerability in the user login form, which allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and access any account, including administrative accounts. Successful exploitation would expose the full customer database and grant the attacker the same access as your trusted users. This issue requires immediate remediation. We also found that the web server is running an outdated version of Apache (2.4.41, released in 2019) with two publicly known security advisories — a software update is recommended within the next maintenance window. Finally, the portal does not set several HTTP security headers (Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options); while these do not introduce direct vulnerabilities, they weaken the browser's defences against future client-side attacks and should be added as part of routine hardening. Full reproduction steps and remediation guidance for each issue follow in the technical findings.' Note what is and is not here: business impact in plain English (no CVSS numbers, no acronyms), priority ordering by risk to the company, no jargon. weeks.title: Defence Basics — Logging, SIEM, Detection
weeks.context:
Security is not only about attack. The other half of the field is defence — detecting, alerting, and responding to attacks. This week you switch to the defender's perspective and learn the core tools: logging, SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), and detection engineering.

Logs are the foundation of security operations. Every login attempt, every HTTP request, every system call generates a log. A SIEM collects logs from across an environment, normalises them, and applies detection rules to find suspicious patterns. Without logs, you cannot detect attacks.

You learn Elastic SIEM (free, open-source) or Splunk (free tier) this week. You ingest logs, write detection queries, and build a basic alert. Even as an offensive security specialist, understanding how defenders detect you makes you a better attacker.

concept_check.q: A log and an alert are not the same thing, and confusing them is the first mistake every junior makes. A log is a passive record — 'user X logged in at 04:02' — written whether or not anyone ever read?
concept_check.explain: See the lesson for explanation. The right answer follows directly from the core idea taught today.

concept_check.q: A false positive is an alert that fires when nothing bad actually happened — the rule matched, but the activity was legitimate. It sounds harmless until you do the arithmetic. Say your SOC processes 1?

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Picture your lab right now: the firewall keeps one log, each VM keeps its own, the web app keeps another — all in different formats, all on different machines. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) is the tool that ingests all of those, normalises them into one common shape so a Windows login and a Linux login become comparable, and then hunts the combined stream for patterns no single box could see alone. The reason this matters is correlation — a failed login here plus a success there plus a file copied somewhere else looks innocent on each machine but screams 'breach' when you line all three up on one timeline. Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel and Elastic are three you will meet in industry, but the tool is the easy part. Tell me in your own words: what can a SIEM detect that you could never spot by reading each machine's logs separately?

weeks.title: Incident Response Basics — When Something Real Happens
weeks.context:
Incidents happen. The question is not whether you will face a security incident but whether you have a plan when you do. Incident Response (IR) is the structured process of detecting, containing, eradicating, and recovering from a security breach.

The IR lifecycle: Preparation → Detection → Analysis → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Post-Incident Review. Most organisations are terrible at Preparation and Post-Incident Review, which means they keep having the same incidents.

This week you learn the IR process, how to triage an incident (what is compromised, how far has it spread, what data is at risk), and how to write a post-incident report. You also learn basic forensics: how to preserve evidence, read system logs, and establish a timeline.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Incident response has a lifecycle, and the discipline is in knowing which phase you are in so you do not, for example, start wiping machines (eradication) before you have figured out how far the attacker spread (analysis). The six phases are Preparation, Detection, Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and the Post-Incident Review — and most organisations are genuinely good at the middle and genuinely terrible at the first and last, which is exactly why they keep suffering the same breach twice. Let's thread one story through it: a developer's laptop gets phished. Preparation is the EDR and the runbook you wrote before it happened; Detection is the alert that fired; Analysis is you scoping what the malware touched; Containment is isolating that laptop; Eradication is removing the implant; Recovery is safely bringing the user back online; and the Review is the meeting where you ask why the phish got through. Take that same phished-laptop scenario and tell me: which phase, done badly, turns a one-laptop incident into a company-wide one?

weeks.title: Endpoint Security — EDR, Hardening, MDM
weeks.context:
Endpoints — laptops, servers, mobile devices — are where most attacks land. Phishing delivers malware to a laptop. A compromised server is an endpoint. Endpoint security is the practice of hardening these devices and monitoring them for malicious activity.

EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) is the modern evolution of antivirus. Instead of signature matching, EDR monitors system behaviour: process creation, network connections, file writes, registry changes. When a process does something suspicious (like spawning PowerShell from Word), the EDR flags it.

This week you learn how defenders harden endpoints (CIS Benchmarks, Group Policy on Windows, sysctl on Linux) and how attackers bypass these controls. Understanding bypass techniques as a defender helps you build better detections.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Traditional antivirus and EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) answer two different questions. Antivirus asks 'have I seen this exact bad file before?' — it matches files against a database of known-malware signatures, which means a brand-new or slightly-modified malware sails straight past it. EDR asks a smarter question: 'is this program behaving like an attacker?' — it watches behaviour, like a Word document spawning PowerShell, or a process reaching into another process's memory, or a binary suddenly making network connections it never made before. The shift matters because modern attackers do not drop a known virus; they abuse legitimate tools and live off the land, which is invisible to signatures but glaring to behavioural monitoring. Give me one concrete attack that AV would completely miss but EDR would catch, and explain what behaviour gives it away.

weeks.title: Threat Intelligence and Hunting
weeks.context:
Threat intelligence is information about adversaries — who they are, what they want, what tools they use, and how they operate. Threat hunting is proactively searching your environment for signs of compromise that automated tools have not detected.

Most security teams are reactive: they respond to alerts. Threat hunters are proactive: they form a hypothesis ('I think an attacker might be using WMI for persistence') and go hunting for evidence of that technique across all their endpoint telemetry.

This week you learn the threat intelligence lifecycle, how to consume and apply threat feeds (IOCs, TTPs), and how to run a basic threat hunt using MITRE ATT&CK as your framework. You also learn about threat actor groups — understanding your likely adversaries changes how you prioritise defences.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Threat intelligence comes in three altitudes, and the mistake is handing the wrong altitude to the wrong person. Strategic intel is the boardroom view — 'ransomware groups are increasingly targeting our industry' — consumed by executives to decide where to spend money. Operational intel is the campaign view — 'this specific group is active and uses these tactics against companies like ours' — consumed by security leadership to prioritise defences. Tactical intel is the trench view — 'here is the exact IP, hash, and command the attacker uses' — consumed by analysts and your SIEM to build detections right now. The same breach generates all three; the skill is translating up and down the ladder. Give me one real threat and write the strategic, operational, and tactical version of it — and tell me who reads each.

weeks.title: Cloud Security — AWS, Azure, GCP
weeks.context:
Cloud infrastructure is now the default for most companies. Cloud security is fundamentally different from on-premise security: the attack surface is configuration, not physical access. Most cloud breaches happen because of misconfigured S3 buckets, overly permissive IAM roles, or exposed metadata endpoints — not because an attacker broke into a data centre.

This week you learn the cloud security fundamentals: shared responsibility model, IAM policies, network security groups, and the most common cloud misconfigurations. You will audit an AWS environment for security issues using tools like ScoutSuite, Prowler, and AWS Config.

The mindset shift: in cloud, your infrastructure is code (Terraform, CloudFormation). Security misconfigurations in that code are vulnerabilities, just like SQL injection in application code.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: The Shared Responsibility Model is the single most misunderstood line in cloud security, and getting it wrong is how companies end up breached while believing 'AWS handles security'. The split is roughly: AWS secures the cloud itself — the physical data centres, the hardware, the hypervisor, the managed-service infrastructure — while you secure what you put in the cloud — your data, your IAM permissions, your network rules, your patching, your S3 bucket settings. The line moves depending on the service: with raw EC2 you patch the OS; with a managed database AWS patches it but you still control who can access it. The dangerous gap is assuming the provider covers something they explicitly do not — like access control on your own data. Pick one AWS service and draw the exact line for me: name one thing AWS secures and one thing that, if you get it wrong, is entirely your breach.

weeks.title: Container and Kubernetes Security
weeks.context:
Container security is now essential because most production workloads run in containers. A container is not a VM — it shares the host kernel. A container escape vulnerability means an attacker who compromises a container can potentially escape to the host and access all other containers.

Kubernetes adds another layer: the API server is the control plane for the entire cluster. A misconfigured RBAC policy or an exposed dashboard can give an attacker cluster-admin access. The 2019 Tesla cryptojacking breach happened because their Kubernetes dashboard had no authentication.

This week you learn container image security (scanning, base image choice), Kubernetes RBAC, Pod Security Standards, network policies, and how to use tools like Trivy, kubeaudit, and kube-bench to audit a cluster.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A container escape is the nightmare scenario of containerisation: an attacker who has compromised the inside of a container breaks out to the host itself — and because every container on that host shares the same kernel, escaping to the host can mean owning every other container too. Remember the core fact that makes this possible: a container is not a VM; it is an isolated process sharing the host's kernel, so a kernel vulnerability or a too-generous configuration is a door out. Two common routes: a runc exploit (a CVE in the container runtime itself), or a misconfigured privileged container or mounted host filesystem/Docker socket that hands the attacker host access by design. Name two escape techniques and tell me, for one of them, whether it is a bug you patch or a configuration you should never have made.

weeks.title: DevSecOps — Security Throughout the SDLC
weeks.context:
DevSecOps integrates security into every phase of the software development lifecycle — not as a gate at the end, but as a continuous practice. The goal: find and fix security issues as early as possible, when they are cheapest to fix.

The DevSecOps toolchain has four layers: SAST (Static Application Security Testing — analysing source code for vulnerabilities without executing it), DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing — attacking a running app), SCA (Software Composition Analysis — finding vulnerable dependencies), and secrets scanning (finding leaked API keys, passwords).

This week you build a security-aware CI/CD pipeline that runs all four layers on every pull request. A developer should see security feedback in the same place they see test results — in their pull request, before merge.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: SAST and DAST attack the same problem — finding vulnerabilities — from opposite ends. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) reads your source code without running it, so it is great at spotting code-level patterns like a SQL query built by string concatenation, a hardcoded secret, or unsafe deserialisation — and it can do this on every commit, before anything is deployed. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) ignores the code and attacks the running app from the outside like a real hacker, so it is great at finding things that only exist at runtime — authentication flaws, server misconfigurations, broken redirects — that SAST cannot see because they are not in the code. Each is blind where the other sees: SAST cannot tell if a vuln is actually exploitable, DAST cannot tell you which line to fix. Give me one vulnerability SAST catches that DAST misses, and one the reverse — and explain why neither alone is enough.

weeks.title: Threat Modelling — Designing Security Before Code
weeks.context:
Threat modelling is the practice of systematically identifying what can go wrong in a system before you build it. Done well, it shifts security from reactive (finding bugs after shipping) to proactive (designing them out before writing a line of code).

The most widely used methodology is STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. You apply STRIDE to a data flow diagram (DFD) of your system, identify threats at each trust boundary, and design mitigations.

This week you learn to draw DFDs, run STRIDE analysis, and produce a threat model document that engineers can act on. Threat modelling is a skill that makes you valuable at any seniority level — most teams do it poorly or not at all.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Threat modelling starts with a picture, not a checklist — you draw a Data Flow Diagram (DFD) showing how data moves through your system, because you cannot defend what you cannot see. For a login flow — user then browser then web app then database — the interesting part is the trust boundary between the browser (which the attacker fully controls) and your web app (which you control); every byte crossing that line is suspect. Now apply STRIDE at that boundary: Spoofing (can someone impersonate the user? then need authentication), Tampering (can they alter the request in transit? then need TLS/integrity), Repudiation (can they deny acting? then need logging), Information disclosure (can they read others' data? then need authorisation), Denial of Service (can they flood login? then need rate limiting), Elevation of privilege (can a normal user become admin? then need access checks). Draw that DFD for me, mark the browser-to-app boundary, and give me the single most dangerous STRIDE threat at it and your mitigation.

weeks.title: Application Security — SAST, DAST, IAST
weeks.context:
Application security (AppSec) is the discipline of making software secure. This week you go deeper into the testing methodologies: SAST (static analysis of code), DAST (dynamic testing of a running app), and IAST (instrumentation inside a running app that observes its own behaviour).

Each has different coverage: SAST finds code-level issues without running the app (good for injection, hardcoded secrets, insecure patterns); DAST attacks the running app from outside (good for auth issues, injection, misconfigurations); IAST sits inside the app and observes data flows at runtime (best coverage, highest complexity).

You also learn code review for security this week — how to manually review a pull request and identify security issues that no automated tool would catch, like broken business logic.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You already know SAST (reads code, runs early) and DAST (attacks the running app from outside) — IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing) is the third approach that sits inside the running application via instrumentation, watching its actual data flows from within as the app handles real requests. Picture where each lives on the build then test then deploy timeline: SAST runs at the code/CI stage on the source; DAST runs at the test/staging stage against a deployed instance from the outside; IAST runs during testing too but from inside the running app, so it sees both the request and the line of code that handled it. That inside view gives IAST the best accuracy — it can confirm a vuln is real and point to the code — at the cost of complexity and runtime overhead. Draw me the SDLC and place all three, and tell me why IAST's position lets it cut the false positives that plague SAST.

weeks.title: Software Supply Chain Security
weeks.context:
The SolarWinds attack in 2020 compromised 18,000 organisations by injecting malicious code into a trusted software update. The Log4Shell vulnerability in 2021 affected millions of apps because they all used the same dependency. Supply chain security is now one of the top priorities in enterprise security.

Your application's attack surface is not just your code — it includes every npm package, Docker base image, CI/CD tool, and cloud provider you depend on. An attacker who compromises any of these can compromise you.

This week you learn: dependency pinning and verification, SBOM (Software Bill of Materials), signed commits and releases, provenance and reproducible builds, and how to use tools like Sigstore/cosign to cryptographically verify the software you consume.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A software supply chain attack compromises you not by attacking your code, but by poisoning something you trust and pull in — a dependency, a base image, a build tool, an update. It is devastating because it inherits your trust: you invited the malicious code in through the front door. SolarWinds in 2020 is the canonical case — attackers breached SolarWinds' build pipeline and slipped malicious code into a legitimate, digitally-signed update of their Orion product, which then auto-deployed to roughly 18,000 customers who had every reason to trust it. The lesson is that 'we secured our code' is not enough when your attack surface includes everyone you depend on. Describe the SolarWinds mechanism back to me in three sentences, and tell me which link in your own build chain a SolarWinds-style attacker would target.

weeks.title: Compliance — SOC2, ISO27001, GDPR
weeks.context:
Compliance is how organisations demonstrate their security posture to customers, regulators, and auditors. It is not security itself — a fully compliant organisation can still be breached. But compliance frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR) encode security best practices that, when implemented honestly, meaningfully reduce risk.

For a security engineer, understanding compliance is essential because it translates business requirements into technical controls. An enterprise customer saying 'do you have SOC 2 Type II?' means 'can you prove your security controls have operated continuously for at least 6 months?'

This week you learn the major frameworks, how to map your technical controls to compliance requirements, and how to prepare for and support an audit.

Zero Trust is the modern security architecture principle: never trust, always verify. It rejects the old perimeter model (trust everything inside the network) and replaces it with: authenticate and authorise every request, every time, regardless of network location.

The practical implementation of Zero Trust involves: strong identity verification (MFA, hardware keys), device health checks, least-privilege access, micro-segmentation (network policies that limit lateral movement), and continuous monitoring. Every access decision is made based on identity + device health + context, not IP address.

This week you learn Zero Trust architecture principles, how to implement them with tools like Tailscale (mesh VPN), Cloudflare Access (identity-aware proxy), and how to design access control systems that are both secure and usable.

## Deeper dive: SSO

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **SSO** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Zero Trust's slogan 'never trust, always verify' is best understood by contrast with the model it replaced. The old perimeter model worked like a castle: a hard wall (the firewall) around the network, and everything inside was trusted — so once an attacker breached the wall (one phished laptop), they could move freely, because the inside was a soft, trusting interior. Zero Trust throws out 'inside means trusted': every request is authenticated and authorised individually, every time, based on identity plus device health plus context, regardless of whether it comes from the office network or a cafe. Network location stops being a credential. Explain to me why the castle model fails the moment one device inside is compromised, and what Zero Trust does differently that contains that same compromised device.

weeks.title: Forensics and Malware Analysis Basics
weeks.context:
Digital forensics is the practice of recovering and analysing evidence from digital systems. Malware analysis is the reverse-engineering of malicious software to understand how it works. Together, they form the investigative backbone of incident response — you need both to answer "what happened, how, and what did the attacker do?"

Static analysis: examine a file without running it (strings, file type, hash, PE headers, disassembly). Dynamic analysis: run the malware in an isolated sandbox and observe what it does (network connections, file writes, registry changes, process creation). You start with static analysis for safety — you never run unknown malware on your own machine.

This week you learn basic forensics workflows, how to use ANY.RUN or Cuckoo for sandboxed malware analysis, and how to use Volatility for memory forensics. You also learn the basics of the Windows PE format — understanding the format helps you detect packed or obfuscated malware.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Static and dynamic analysis are the two halves of examining a suspect file, and the order matters for your safety. Static analysis examines the file without running it — you look at its strings, file type, hashes, headers, and disassembly to learn what it might do. Dynamic analysis runs it in an isolated sandbox and watches what it actually does — network connections, files written, registry changes, processes spawned. You always start static, for one blunt reason: you never execute unknown malware until you know something about it, because running it is exactly what the attacker wants, and a sandbox escape or a missed network call could infect your real environment. Tell me three things static analysis reveals before you would ever consider running the sample, and what dynamic analysis adds that static can never tell you.

weeks.title: Tabletop Exercises and Red Teaming
weeks.context:
A tabletop exercise is a structured discussion where a team works through a simulated security incident. No systems are touched — it is a meeting. The value is in discovering gaps in your response process, communication chains, and decision-making before a real incident happens.

Red teaming is an adversarial simulation where a skilled team tries to compromise an organisation's defences using real attack techniques, with full scope and duration (days to weeks, not hours). Red team engagements are distinct from pentests: pentests find as many vulnerabilities as possible; red teams test whether defenders can detect and respond to a realistic attack.

This week you learn to run a basic tabletop exercise, understand the structure of a red team engagement, and learn about adversary simulation frameworks (Atomic Red Team, CALDERA) that let you safely simulate specific ATT&CK techniques in your own lab.

## Key ideas

items.title: Deeper dive: Atomic Red Team
items.body:
## Deeper dive: Atomic Red Team

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **Atomic Red Team** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: These three exercises test your defences at very different costs and depths. A tabletop exercise is a meeting — no systems are touched; the team talks through a simulated incident to find gaps in process, communication, and decision-making ('who calls legal? who decides to pull the plug?'). A red team engagement is the opposite extreme — a skilled adversarial team actually attacks your live environment over days or weeks, with real techniques, to test whether your defenders detect and respond. A purple team sits in between and collaborative: red and blue work together in real time, the attacker runs a technique and the defender immediately checks 'did we see that?', tuning detections on the spot. Lay out the three for me on a scale of cost and realism, and tell me which one you would run first in an org that has never tested its defences, and why.

weeks.title: Building a Career in Security — Specialisation + Portfolio
weeks.context:
Security is a broad field and no one masters all of it. The people who get hired and promoted are specialists with a visible track record. This week you decide your specialisation, build your public portfolio, and learn how to navigate the security job market.

The main specialisation tracks: offensive security (pentesting, red team, bug bounty), defensive security (SOC analyst, detection engineer, incident response), cloud security, AppSec, GRC (governance, risk, compliance), and malware/threat intelligence. Each has different certifications, job titles, and career paths.

Your portfolio is your proof of work. A GitHub with CTF writeups, a blog with vulnerability research, and a list of CVEs or bug bounty findings is more valuable than any certification. Certifications validate that you have studied; portfolio proves you can do.

## What it is
LinkedIn profile + GitHub portfolio repo is the foundation for this week's work. Without it installed and working, every later day will fail with a cryptic error.

## What you'll do today

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for **free**, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **AWS** — use **LocalStack** (mocks AWS APIs on your laptop) plus **MinIO** (local S3). The CLI commands are the same; set `--endpoint-url=http://localhost:4566`. No AWS account or card required.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

## Context
This applies specifically to week 23 ('Building a Career in Security — Specialisation + Portfolio'), day 0.

weeks.title: Capstone — Earn It
weeks.context:
You have spent 24 weeks learning how to think like an attacker, communicate like a professional, defend like an engineer, and build a career in security. The capstone is not a test — it is a proof of work that demonstrates all of this in a form that is visible to employers and the community.

You will complete three deliverables: a full vulnerability report from a real bug bounty programme or a self-hosted lab environment, a public write-up (blog post) of a technique or finding, and a security portfolio document that ties together everything you have built.

No shortcuts. No AI-generated findings. Every vulnerability you report must be one you found yourself, understood fully, and can explain in detail. The capstone is the start of your career, not the end of a course.

## What it is
Full sec toolchain check (Kali, Burp, ZAP, Metasploit, Prowler) is the foundation for this week's work. Without it installed and working, every later day will fail with a cryptic error.

prowler -v

You will complete three deliverables: a full vulnerability report from a real bug bounty programme or a self-hosted lab environment, a public write-up (blog post) of a technique or finding, and a security p

## Key ideas

items.title: Deeper dive: The first 90 days of your next security role
items.body:
## Deeper dive: The first 90 days of your next security role

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **The first 90 days of your next security role** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.
